item.title: Elbow — Joint Mobilization
clinicalUse: Use when assessment identifies a relevant impairment in Elbow and the parent technique fits the patient's presentation.
Primary treatment target: elbow flexion/extension, forearm rotation, grip and load-related pain.
Retain the technique only if it produces a meaningful within-session improvement.
patientPosition: Sitting or supine with the upper limb supported.
Keep wrist and shoulder relaxed unless movement is part of the technique.
therapistPosition: Stand or sit beside the arm with the elbow supported close to the body.
stabilization: Stabilize humerus or forearm according to the target joint/tissue.
contact: Use broad contact around the ulnohumeral/radiocapitellar region or target soft tissue; protect the ulnar nerve and radial head region.
Select the joint surface/accessory motion that best relates to the patient's comparable sign.
Use a comfortable broad contact and localize the intended segment rather than moving the whole region.
forceDirection: Apply rhythmic Grade I–IV oscillation according to pain, stiffness and irritability.
Direction is chosen from the joint mechanics and, more importantly, the immediate clinical response.
dosage: A common trial is 30–60 seconds for 2–4 bouts with reassessment after each bout.
steps: 1. Record the exact comparable sign for Elbow: elbow flexion/extension, forearm rotation, grip and load-related pain.
2. Screen regional red flags, contraindications and technique-specific precautions before touching the patient.
3. Position and stabilize the patient so the target is comfortable and the manual input can be localized.
4. Apply a low-force trial using the parent technique principles and the region-specific contact described above.
5. Monitor pain quality, symptom distribution, guarding and patient confidence throughout.
6. Re-test the original comparable sign immediately after the trial.
7. Keep the technique only when the response is useful, then transfer the gain into active movement, loading or self-management.
mistakes: Applying the technique because it is familiar rather than because the examination supports it.
Using more force when the response is unclear or worsening.
Failing to re-test the exact movement or function that justified the treatment.
safety: Avoid aggressive treatment with suspected fracture, unstable ligament injury, acute nerve irritation or major swelling.
Stop or modify if symptoms peripheralize, neurological status worsens, the response is disproportionate or the patient asks to stop.
item.visualCue: Elbow assessment → correct regional setup → Joint Mobilization → immediate comparable-sign re-test.

subTechniques.name: Ulnohumeral Distraction
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Reduce compression sensitivity and prepare flexion/extension in a stiff or painful elbow.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Supine or sitting with the arm supported and elbow in a comfortable loose-packed position.
subTechniques.contact: Stabilize the distal humerus and grasp the proximal ulna/forearm securely while protecting the ulnar nerve.
subTechniques.direction: Apply gentle long-axis distraction through the ulnohumeral joint.
subTechniques.dosage: 10–30 second holds or Grade I–II oscillatory distraction × 3–5 trials.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: Keep the traction close to the joint; pulling the wrist mainly tensions the forearm.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Avoid acute dislocation, fracture or unstable ligament injury.

subTechniques.name: Radial Head AP / PA Glide
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Improve pronation/supination when radial-head accessory motion is restricted.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Sitting or supine with elbow supported in slight flexion.
subTechniques.contact: Stabilize the ulna/humerus and contact the radial head precisely, avoiding excessive pressure on the posterior interosseous nerve region.
subTechniques.direction: Apply a small anterior or posterior glide chosen from the restricted forearm rotation and immediate response.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: The radial head is small—precision matters more than force.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Stop with nerve-type pain, tingling or acute lateral-elbow instability.
